analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal aid to career education programs that leave students with heavy debt and poor earnings, and strengthens protections for student borrowers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2025 with two Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate education committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make career education programs prove their graduates earn enough to handle their debt — programs that fail the test two years out of three would lose access to federal student aid for three years. It would make it easier for students misled by a school to get their federal loans wiped out, guarantee automatic loan discharge when a school closes, ban forced arbitration and transcript-withholding over unpaid balances, require colleges to spend at least 30% of tuition revenue on actual instruction, and create a new enforcement office plus a multi-agency committee to police for-profit colleges.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and graduates of career education programs, especially at for-profit colleges, who would face lower risk of enrolling in a worthless program, easier loan discharge if they were misled or their school closed, and new rights in court. Taxpayers also benefit, since the same students' unpaid debts currently fall on the federal government.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts off federal student aid to career-education programs whose graduates carry debt loads their earnings cannot support, measured by debt-to-earnings and earnings-premium tests.

Lets defrauded borrowers have their loans discharged, including through a group process when a school's misrepresentations were widespread, and requires automatic discharge for students of schools that close.

Bars schools from forcing students into arbitration or away from court, and from withholding transcripts over an unpaid balance — a practice that blocks former students from transferring or getting jobs.

Requires colleges to spend at least 30% of tuition revenue on actual instruction rather than marketing and recruitment, and creates an enforcement unit in the Department of Education to investigate complaints with subpoena power and higher civil penalties.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit colleges and poor-performing career programs would lose federal student aid revenue, and lenders and investors tied to that sector would bear losses from discharges and terminations. Taxpayers fund the new enforcement apparatus.

drawbacks.text: The debt-to-earnings and earnings-premium tests are one-size-fits-all: a program that fails two of three years loses access to federal aid for at least three years, which could shut down borderline-but-legitimate programs and reduce training options in some fields.
Borrower-defense discharges are broadened and made easier to obtain, and the costs of discharging loans fall partly on taxpayers and on lenders whose guarantees are tied to the loans.

The bill removes normal rulemaking procedures (sections 492) for several major provisions and issues detailed rules directly in statute, reducing the chance for stakeholders to shape the details — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for students and taxpayers are substantial: fewer dollars flowing to programs that leave graduates with debt but no earnings gain, an easier path to loan discharge when schools mislead them, and an end to transcript-withholding and forced arbitration. The costs are real but modest by comparison: schools would face new reporting duties and could lose federal aid, some low-performing programs (and the enrollment they offer) would close, and lenders holding loans guaranteed against default would see more discharges. The main design criticism is that the rules are blunt — a single debt-to-earnings test applied across all sectors could sweep in some worthwhile programs — but the 3-year lookback and appeal-for-calculation-error provisions soften that.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Puppies Committee in March 2025 and has sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 12, 2025 and read twice before being referred to the Senate HELP Committee.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no vote — in the year and more since referral.
It has only two cosponsors, both Democrats, alongside its sponsor and original cosponsors.
The bill would bar federal aid to career education programs that fail debt-to-earnings and earnings-premium tests, a direct hit to a sector that depends on that aid.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges and the loan servicers and contractors that profit from federal student aid are better off because the bill never moved; students at predatory programs and taxpayers who fund loan discharges are not.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 12, 2025 and shepherded its referral to the HELP Committee.

for.name: Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Jeff Merkley

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record.

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.what_they_did: Has historically lobbied intensively against gainful-employment rules and borrower-defense enforcement that threaten its federal aid revenue.

sides.party_line_note: All three named sponsors are Democrats with no Republican cosponsors, and the bill received no committee action in a Senate controlled by Republicans.

industries.industry: For-profit colleges and career education chains
industries.note: The bill's chief target: programs whose graduates' debt loads outstrip earnings would lose federal aid, and the industry faces mandatory instructional-spending minimums, disclosure of marketing spending, and an inter-agency oversight committee aimed squarely at it. Its federal-aid revenue model is directly at risk.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and third-party servicers
industries.note: They would face a new enforcement unit, complaint tracking, expanded program-review scrutiny, and higher civil penalties, and their contracts would require complaint-response compliance.

industries.industry: Traditional public and private nonprofit colleges
industries.note: Most meet the 30% instructional-spending floor easily, but the spending requirement and disclosures apply to all institutions, and graduate and professional programs would also be subject to debt-to-earnings transparency.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in the HELP Committee since March 2025 with two cosponsors and no hearing or markup, and the committee is chaired by the opposing party. Bills at this stage with no committee action and no bipartisan cosponsors almost never reach the floor; the realistic prospect of enactment in this Congress is very low.
